lessons.title: Predicting the Weather

activities.prompt: How can we know what the weather will do before it happens?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Weather and Climate
activities.body: Temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind and atmospheric pressure together define the weather. Meteorologists are people who collect weather data using instruments over long periods. This data helps them monitor and predict the weather. Accurate predictions help us prepare for extreme events. A loo is a strong, hot and dusty wind in northern India during summer. Climate change makes extreme weather more frequent. Weather is closely linked to climate.
keyPoints: Weather data is collected with instruments over long periods.
Data helps monitor and predict the weather.
Accurate predictions help prepare for extreme events.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how weather data and climate help people prepare.

activities.prompt: Ravi's village is by the sea. The radio says stormy weather is coming soon. Should the fishermen take their boats out today?
steps: Stormy weather is made of wind, rain and other weather parts together.
Accurate predictions tell us about these parts before they arrive.
Fishermen are warned not to go out when stormy weather is expected.
So staying on land keeps them safe, since storms can be dangerous at sea.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: What do meteorologists use to collect weather data?
options: Instruments
Boats
Paintings
Gardens
activities.explanation: They use instruments to collect weather data over long periods.

activities.prompt: Meteorologists collect weather data only once.
activities.explanation: Meteorologists collect data over long periods, not only once.

activities.prompt: Meteorologists collect data over ______ periods of time.
activities.hint: Think about how long the collection continues.
activities.explanation: Weather data is collected over long periods for better predictions.

activities.prompt: Put these weather-preparation steps in order.
items: Use data to monitor the weather
activities.explanation: Instrument data supports weather predictions, which help governments prepare resources.

activities.prompt: A forecast shows stormy weather. What should a fisherman do?
options: Stay ashore
Go out in a boat
Ignore the warning
Prepare cyclone resources
activities.explanation: Fishermen can be warned not to go out when stormy weather is expected.

activities.prompt: Match each weather situation with the useful response.
pairs: Warn fishermen not to go out
activities.explanation: Weather data supports predictions that help people, governments and fishermen prepare.

activities.prompt: A weather station has recorded rain for many years. Meena's teacher says these records help make better predictions. Why do many years of records help?
options: They show patterns in how the weather changes over time.
They stop rain from falling on the same place again.
They tell the exact rain for every hour next year.
They show rain only on the hottest days of the year.

why.They stop rain from falling on the same: Wrong: this thinks records control the rain, but records only collect data.
why.They tell the exact rain for every hour: Wrong: this thinks records make perfect predictions, but predictions are never exact to the hour.
why.They show rain only on the hottest days: Wrong: this thinks only hot days matter, but records help us study all the weather.

activities.explanation: Right: long records show patterns, so predictions can be more accurate.

activities.prompt: In Meena's village, rain is the strongest part of the weather in July. Her father is a farmer. He must plan his work for the month. What should he plan around?
options: Wind, because wind is the most important part every month.
Temperature, because heat is always the strongest part of weather.
Rain, because rain is the strongest part of the weather in July.
Nothing, because no part of the weather can be strongest.

why.Wind, because wind is the most important: Wrong: this thinks one weather part is always the strongest, but it changes with the time.
why.Temperature, because heat is always the: Wrong: this thinks heat always leads, but in July rain is the dominant part.
why.Nothing, because no part of the weather: Wrong: this thinks all weather parts are equal, but one part can be dominant at a time.

activities.explanation: Right: rain is dominant in July, so it matters most for his plans.

activities.prompt: Ravi's aunt lives in northern India. She says: 'All summer afternoon, a hot, dusty wind pushed sand into our house.' Which weather event is she describing?
options: A cyclone, because a strong wind means a big storm.
A loo, because a hot dusty wind blows there in summer.
A flood, because a lot of water covers the roads.
A drought, because the land stays dry for a long time.

why.A cyclone, because a strong wind means a: Wrong: this thinks any strong wind is a cyclone, but she describes a hot, dusty wind.
why.A flood, because a lot of water covers t: Wrong: this thinks any bad weather is a flood, but she describes wind, not water.
why.A drought, because the land stays dry fo: Wrong: this thinks any dry weather is a drought, but she describes a hot, dusty wind.

activities.explanation: Right: a loo is a strong, hot, dusty wind that blows in northern India in summer.

activities.prompt: The weather office predicts a cyclone will reach a coastal town soon. The local government wants to prepare resources. Which action helps most?
options: Wait until the cyclone hits, then send help to the town.
Store food, water and boats in safe places before the cyclone comes.
Cancel the warnings, because the cyclone might never reach us.
Ignore the forecast, because predictions are not always perfect.

why.Wait until the cyclone hits, then send h: Wrong: this waits too long, so there is no time to prepare resources.
why.Cancel the warnings, because the cyclone: Wrong: this thinks an uncertain event will not happen, so people stay unready.
why.Ignore the forecast, because predictions: Wrong: this thinks an imperfect prediction is useless, but it still helps us prepare.

activities.explanation: Right: accurate predictions let leaders prepare resources before a disaster.

activities.context: A school has a small weather station in its playground. Its thermometer uses a coloured liquid that expands when the temperature rises, and it records the day's maximum and minimum temperatures. Beside it is a rain gauge. Rain falls into a funnel and is collected in a cylinder, where a scale shows the depth of the water. After a shower, the scale reads 5 millimetres. A second, digital thermometer shows 15 degrees Celsius at the same time.
activities.prompt: If the air around the thermometer becomes warmer during the afternoon, what will the coloured liquid most likely do?
options: It shrinks, so the column drops lower in the tube.
It takes up more space, so the column climbs higher.
It stays the same height, because only the scale changes.
It turns solid, so the column stops moving.

why.It shrinks, so the column drops lower in: Wrong: the liquid grows in warm air, so it does not shrink.
why.It stays the same height, because only t: Wrong: the liquid itself responds to temperature; the scale does not change the reading.
why.It turns solid, so the column stops movi: Wrong: the liquid does not freeze on a warm afternoon, so it keeps moving.

activities.explanation: Right: as the temperature rises, the liquid takes up more space and climbs.

activities.context: A school has a small weather station in its playground. Its thermometer uses a coloured liquid that expands when the temperature rises, and it records the day's maximum and minimum temperatures. Beside it is a rain gauge. Rain falls into a funnel and is collected in a cylinder, where a scale shows the depth of the water. After a shower, the scale reads 5 millimetres. A second, digital thermometer shows 15 degrees Celsius at the same time.
activities.prompt: A visitor's guide gives a temperature of 59 degrees Fahrenheit, while the school thermometer reads 15 degrees Celsius. What should the student conclude?
options: The guide's day is hotter, because 59 is a bigger number than 15.
The two readings show the same temperature, because the two scales measure one value in different units.
The guide's reading is wrong, because Fahrenheit numbers are always smaller.
The readings differ, so the student should add them together to get one value.

why.The guide's day is hotter, because 59 is: Wrong: the numbers belong to different scales, so their size does not compare the temperatures.
why.The guide's reading is wrong, because Fa: Wrong: Fahrenheit numbers are not always smaller; the two scales simply differ.
why.The readings differ, so the student shou: Wrong: adding readings from two different scales gives no meaningful temperature.

activities.explanation: Right: both readings describe the same temperature, expressed in different units.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a thermometer that measures the surrounding temperature and one that records daily maximum and minimum temperatures?
activities.answer: A surrounding-temperature thermometer shows the temperature at the moment it is read. A maximum and minimum thermometer records the highest and lowest temperatures reached during the day, so the class can later work out the temperature range or mean daily temperature.
points: Surrounding-temperature thermometer shows the current temperature
Maximum and minimum thermometer records the highest and lowest temperatures of the day
Maximum and minimum readings allow the temperature range or mean daily temperature to be calculated
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a barometer and a hygrometer?
activities.answer: A barometer is the instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure, which is the pressure exerted by the weight of the air above and around us. A hygrometer is the instrument used to measure humidity, which is the amount of water vapour present in the air.
points: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure
A hygrometer measures humidity
Pressure comes from the weight of air; humidity is water vapour in the air
Each instrument measures a different thing
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A fishing village on a coast receives a warning from meteorologists that a cyclone is likely. Their predictions rely on instruments that have recorded data over long periods of time. Because the forecast is accurate, the local government has prepared relief resources and safe shelters. Fishermen have been advised not to go out to sea when stormy weather is expected. Many of them are staying at home.
activities.prompt: If the fishermen had not received this advice, what would most likely have happened?
options: They would have sailed out unaware and been caught in the cyclone.
They would have stayed safely ashore because the sky looked clear.
The local government would have stopped recording data with its instruments.
The cyclone would have been weaker because nobody was warned about it.

why.They would have stayed safely ashore bec: Wrong: the advice concerns predicted stormy weather, not the appearance of the sky.
why.The local government would have stopped: Wrong: instruments record data regardless of whether anyone is warned.
why.The cyclone would have been weaker becau: Wrong: a warning does not change how strong a cyclone is.

activities.explanation: Correct: without a warning, the fishermen would not know the danger.

activities.context: A fishing village on a coast receives a warning from meteorologists that a cyclone is likely. Their predictions rely on instruments that have recorded data over long periods of time. Because the forecast is accurate, the local government has prepared relief resources and safe shelters. Fishermen have been advised not to go out to sea when stormy weather is expected. Many of them are staying at home.
activities.prompt: If cyclones become more frequent because of climate change, what is the best step for the local government?
options: Stop recording instrument readings, since storms cannot be predicted at all.
Keep gathering long-term data and plan shelters for more frequent extreme storms.
Reduce warnings so fishermen are not disturbed while they work.
Wait for cyclones to become rare again before preparing any resources.

why.Stop recording instrument readings, sinc: Wrong: data collected with instruments helps us predict the weather.
why.Reduce warnings so fishermen are not dis: Wrong: warnings protect fishermen, so reducing them increases danger.
why.Wait for cyclones to become rare again b: Wrong: climate change makes extreme weather more frequent, not rarer.

activities.explanation: Correct: long-term data and preparation help face more frequent extreme events.

options: Air's state at one time and place
Lowest atmospheric layer near the ground
Air movement with speed and direction
Water vapour amount present in the air

activities.prompt: The troposphere is the layer where land plants and animals live.
activities.explanation: The troposphere is closest to the Earth's surface. Land plants and animals live there.

activities.prompt: Which instrument measures humidity?

Hygrometer
Barometer
Anemometer

activities.explanation: Wind moves from areas of high pressure towards areas of low pressure.

activities.explanation: The weight of the air creates pressure. A barometer is used to measure it.

chapters.title: Climates of India
chapters.summary: In this chapter: weather, seasons and climate; types of climates in india; factors determining the climate; the monsoons.

lessons.title: Weather, Seasons and Climate

activities.prompt: Curious about what makes weather, climate, and seasons so different?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Weather and Climate
activities.body: Weather changes from hour to hour and keeps changing. Climate is the long-term pattern of a region's weather. Seasons happen because Earth travels around the Sun. Each lasts for a few months and returns every year. Spring, summer, monsoon, autumn and winter form a cycle. Many parts of India use six seasons called ṛitus. Human actions have recently caused climate changes.
keyPoints: Weather keeps changing from hour to hour.
Climate is a region's long-term weather pattern.
Seasons form a yearly cycle around the Sun.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main ideas of the lesson.

activities.prompt: Maya wakes up cold. By lunchtime, it is hot and sunny. Why did the weather change so fast?
steps: Weather is what the air is like at one time of day.
Weather can change many times within a single day.
Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a place, not one day.
So Maya's quick change is weather, not climate.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Seasons and Life
activities.body: Seasons are linked with both weather and climate. The seasonal pattern of a region is closely connected with its climate. Many parts of India divide the year into six ṛitus. Rituals and festivals are linked with these ṛitus. Plant and animal life follows the rhythm of the ṛitus or seasons.
keyPoints: A region's seasons are closely connected with its climate.
Some Indian regions use six ṛitus.
Rituals, festivals and living things follow seasonal rhythms.
activities.explanation: These connections help us understand life around the seasons.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes climate?
options: A long-term weather pattern
Weather that changes each hour
A season lasting a few months
A festival linked to a season
activities.explanation: Climate is the long-term pattern of a region's weather. Weather itself changes from hour to hour.

activities.prompt: The long-term pattern of a region's weather is called ______.
activities.hint: This word describes weather over many years.
activities.explanation: Climate means the long-term pattern of a region's weather.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an idea and its meaning from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these seasons in their cycle order.
activities.explanation: These seasons occur in a cycle and return every year.

activities.prompt: What causes seasons to happen?
options: Earth travelling around the Sun
Changes in weather each hour
Human actions changing climate
Long-term patterns in a region
activities.explanation: Seasons occur because Earth revolves around the Sun. This is called travelling around the Sun.

activities.prompt: A region's plants and animals follow its seasonal rhythm. Which idea connects closely?
options: The region's climate
The hourly weather
Human actions now
Recent weather changes
activities.explanation: A region's seasonal pattern is closely connected with its climate. Living things follow this seasonal rhythm.

activities.prompt: Noor's class learns that the Earth goes around the Sun. Noor asks why the same season comes back every year. Which answer makes sense?
options: The Earth keeps going around the Sun each year.
The Sun goes around the Earth each year.
Clouds cover the Sun in the same months each year.
Weather stops in one season and starts again.

Wrong. This reverses the Earth and Sun. The Earth is the one that moves.
why.Clouds cover the Sun in the same months: Wrong. Clouds are weather. They do not make the yearly cycle.
why.Weather stops in one season and starts a: Wrong. Weather changes all the time. It does not stop in one season.

activities.explanation: Right. Each trip around the Sun brings the seasons back again.

activities.prompt: Town A had rain on Monday and sun on Tuesday. Town B has had rain every July for many years. Which town's pattern shows its climate?
options: Town B, because its rain comes in a steady yearly pattern.
Town A, because its weather changed in two days.
Town A, because it had both rain and sun.
Town B, because it rained in July this year.

why.Town A, because its weather changed in t: Wrong. Quick changes are weather, not climate. This mixes up the two.
why.Town A, because it had both rain and sun: Wrong. Rain and sun in one week is weather, not a long pattern.
why.Town B, because it rained in July this y: Wrong. One year of rain is weather. Climate needs many years to show.

activities.explanation: Right. Climate is a long pattern, and Town B repeats its rain each year.

activities.prompt: Ben says a very hot week proves that the climate has changed. Why is Ben's idea weak?
options: A hot week is weather, not a long-term pattern.
Hot weeks never happen in any climate.
Climate changes only come from the Sun.
A hot week shows the Earth stopped moving.

Wrong. Weather changes, so a hot week can happen. That alone does not show climate change.
Wrong. Recent climate changes come from human actions, not only the Sun.
why.A hot week shows the Earth stopped movin: Wrong. The Earth still goes around the Sun. A hot week does not stop that.

activities.explanation: Right. Climate is the long pattern. One hot week is only weather.

lessons.title: Types of Climates in India

activities.prompt: Why does India’s weather feel so different from place to place?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Climate Types
activities.body: India has several climate types. An alpine climate has cold, snowy winters and cool summers. A temperate climate has moderately cold winters and mild summers. A subtropical climate has very hot summers and cold winters. An arid climate has very little rainfall. A semi-arid climate has moderate rainfall and mild winters. A tropical climate has distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds.
keyPoints: Alpine climates have snowy winters and cool summers.
Arid climates have very little rainfall.
Tropical climates have wet and dry periods.
activities.explanation: These clues help you identify India's different climates.

activities.prompt: Riya packs for two trips. One is to the Himalayas. The other is to the Thar Desert. Why does she pack thicker clothes for the Himalayas?
steps: The Himalayas have cold, snowy winters and cool summers.
Cold weather means thick clothes help a person stay warm.
The Thar Desert has extremely hot days, but its nights are cool.
So the Himalayas feel colder overall, and Riya needs thicker clothes there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Monsoon and the Tropical Climate
activities.body: A tropical climate has distinct wet and dry periods. Monsoon winds control these periods. The western coastal strip receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon months. A tropical wet climate is favourable for growing rice and spices. Eastern India and the southern peninsula have a tropical climate.
keyPoints: Monsoon winds control wet and dry periods.
The western coast receives heavy monsoon rainfall.
Tropical wet climates suit rice and spices.
activities.explanation: You can now connect monsoons with rainfall and tropical farming.

activities.prompt: What is the climate of the northern plains?
options: A subtropical climate
A mild temperate climate
A snowy alpine climate
A dry desert climate
activities.explanation: The northern plains have very hot summers and cold winters.

activities.prompt: The Himalayan mountains have cold, snowy winters under an alpine climate.
activities.explanation: Yes! Alpine areas have cold, snowy winters and cool summers.

activities.prompt: Many hilly areas have a ______ climate with moderately cold winters.
activities.hint: Its summers are not too hot.
activities.explanation: A temperate climate has moderately cold winters and summers that are not too hot.

activities.prompt: Match each place with its climate feature.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each place has its own climate pattern.

activities.prompt: What controls the wet and dry periods in eastern India and the southern peninsula?
options: Monsoon winds control the wet and dry periods.
Alpine snow controls the wet and dry periods.
Arid heat controls the wet and dry periods.
Cold winters control the wet and dry periods.
activities.explanation: Yes! Their tropical climate has wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds.

activities.prompt: Match each region with its stated climate feature.
pairs: cold, snowy winters and cool summers
very hot summers and cold winters
extremely hot days and cool nights
hot summers, mild winters and moderate rainfall
eastern India and the southern peninsula
activities.explanation: Excellent! You matched each region with its correct climate feature.

activities.prompt: Asha lives in a hill town with moderately cold winters. Her cousin lives on the northern plains. Whose summers are hotter?
options: Asha's, because hills are closer to the sun.
Asha's, because hilly areas get very hot summers.
Her cousin's, because the northern plains have very hot summers.
They are the same, because both places are in India.

why.Asha's, because hills are closer to the: Wrong: she thinks higher land always means more heat.
why.Asha's, because hilly areas get very hot: Wrong: she mixes up hilly areas, which are not too hot, with very hot places.
why.They are the same, because both places a: Wrong: she thinks one country always has one single climate.

activities.explanation: Right: the northern plains have very hot summers and cold winters.

activities.prompt: A farmer in the Thar Desert and a farmer on the western coast both want to grow rice. Which farmer will find it easier?
options: The coast farmer, because its wet climate suits rice growing.
The desert farmer, because its strong sun helps every crop.
Both farmers, because rice grows well anywhere in India.
Neither farmer, because rice needs cold, snowy winters.

why.The desert farmer, because its strong su: Wrong: she thinks strong sun alone is enough for a crop.
why.Both farmers, because rice grows well an: Wrong: she thinks the climate of a place does not matter for crops.
why.Neither farmer, because rice needs cold,: Wrong: she mixes up rice with the snowy climate of the mountains.

activities.explanation: Right: the coast gets heavy monsoon rain, and wet tropical climates suit rice.

activities.prompt: Leela's village gets heavy rain in June, but almost no rain in March. What causes this change?
options: Monsoon winds that blow in some months and not others.
Snow melting from the mountains every June.
Cold winters that stop the rain from falling.
Hot summers that dry up all the rain.

why.Snow melting from the mountains every Ju: Wrong: he thinks mountain snow feeds the rain in every village.
why.Cold winters that stop the rain from fal: Wrong: he thinks the cold season is what stops rain from falling.
Wrong: he thinks heat removes all the rain from the sky.

activities.explanation: Right: a tropical climate has wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds.

lessons.title: Factors Determining the Climate

activities.prompt: Why do some places feel hotter, colder, wetter, or windier than others?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Shapes a Region's Climate?
activities.body: Your book says that several factors work together to shape a region's climate. Low latitudes are warmer, while polar regions receive less heat. As altitude increases, temperature, air pressure, and air density decrease. Moving inland can make temperatures more extreme. Winds affect temperature, humidity, and precipitation. Sea winds may bring moisture and rainfall. The Himalayas and Karakoram partly protect the Indian subcontinent from cold desert winds. A microclimate is a small area with a climate different from its surroundings.
keyPoints: Latitude, altitude, distance from the coast, and winds affect climate.
The Himalayas and Karakoram partly protect the Indian subcontinent.
A microclimate differs from the surrounding region.
activities.explanation: Many factors work together to shape a region's climate.

activities.prompt: A climber reaches the top of a tall hill. The climber feels much colder there. Why?
steps: The top of the hill is higher than the bottom.
Temperature gets lower as altitude goes up.
So the top is colder, because height changes the temperature.
Altitude, not nearness to the Equator, is the reason the top feels colder.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: Which place is warmer?
options: Near the Equator
Near a polar region
At high altitude
Far inland
activities.explanation: Places near the Equator are warmer because they are at low latitudes.

activities.prompt: Temperature decreases as altitude ______.
activities.hint: Think about moving to a higher place.
activities.explanation: Temperature decreases as altitude increases.

activities.prompt: Match each place or change with its climate effect.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how a factor changes temperature or heat.

activities.prompt: What may happen when winds come from the sea?
options: They bring moisture over land.
They always cause drought.
They make air pressure rise.
They stop rainfall.
activities.explanation: Winds from the sea bring moisture over land and may cause rainfall.

activities.prompt: Put the sea-wind process in order.
activities.explanation: Sea winds carry moisture over land, and this moisture may cause rainfall.

activities.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: Many factors shape a region's climate.
One factor alone shapes a region's climate.
A microclimate matches its surroundings.
A polar region is a microclimate.
activities.explanation: A region's climate is determined collectively by all these factors. A microclimate differs from its surrounding region.

activities.prompt: A family drives from the bottom of a hill to its top. What happens to the temperature?
options: It gets warmer, because the top is closer to the sun.
It gets colder, because altitude goes up as they climb.
It stays the same, because the hill is on land.
It gets warmer first, then colder again as they climb.

why.It gets warmer, because the top is close: Wrong: it assumes a higher place must be warmer, which is not how altitude works.
why.It stays the same, because the hill is o: Wrong: it thinks all land has the same temperature, but height changes it.
why.It gets warmer first, then colder again: Wrong: it thinks temperature rises and falls like a wave as you climb.

activities.explanation: Right: temperature decreases as altitude increases, so the top is colder.

activities.prompt: Two cities are at the same latitude. City X is by the sea. City Y is far inland. Which city has more extreme temperatures?
options: City X, since the sea is nearby.
City Y, since it is far from the sea.
Both, since they have the same latitude.
City X, since the sea always heats the air.

Wrong: it thinks being near the sea makes temperatures extreme.
Wrong: it thinks the same latitude means the same temperatures, ignoring the coast.
why.City X, since the sea always heats the a: Wrong: it thinks the sea always heats the air, which is not the rule.

activities.explanation: Right: moving inland from the coast makes temperatures more extreme.

activities.prompt: A village lies behind high mountain ranges. Cold desert winds blow toward the area. The village is less cold than nearby land. Why?
options: The village is very near the Equator.
The sea is sending warm winds to the village.
The village is at a very high altitude, so it is warm.
High mountain ranges block some cold desert winds.

Wrong: it thinks being near the Equator is the only reason for less cold.
why.The sea is sending warm winds to the vil: Wrong: it thinks sea winds are the reason, but the mountains are what protect it.
why.The village is at a very high altitude,: Wrong: it thinks high altitude makes a place warm, but temperature falls with height.

activities.explanation: Right: the ranges protect the area partly from cold desert winds.

lessons.title: The Monsoons

activities.prompt: Why do monsoon winds change direction, and where does their rain fall?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Monsoons Work
activities.body: Monsoon season is central to India's life. Monsoon means seasonal winds over a large area of the Indian Ocean region. Land heats and cools faster than the ocean. Air always flows from high pressure towards low pressure. In summer, hot Asian land creates low pressure. Ocean winds carry moisture over warmer land, causing heavy monsoon rain. In winter, the pressure pattern reverses, and dry winds blow from land to ocean.
keyPoints: The summer monsoon is called the southwest monsoon because of the wind direction.
Monsoon rains usually advance from southern India in early June.
The Western Ghats give their western slopes much more rainfall.
Some winter winds bring rainfall to eastern and southern India.
activities.explanation: Changing land pressure changes the direction of India's monsoon winds.

activities.prompt: Why does wet wind blow from the sea onto the land in summer?
steps: In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean.
So the hot land creates a low-pressure area over it.
Air always flows from high pressure towards low pressure.
So moist ocean winds blow onto the land and bring heavy monsoon rain.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: What Does Monsoon Mean?
activities.prompt: Which meaning fits the word monsoon?
options: Seasonal winds over the Indian Ocean region
Rain that falls only in winter months
Land that stays hot throughout the year
A mountain barrier for strong ocean winds
activities.explanation: Monsoon means seasonal winds over a large area of the Indian Ocean region.

activities.title: Summer Pressure
activities.prompt: During summer, hot Asian land creates a powerful ______-pressure system.
activities.hint: This is the pressure type created by hot land.
activities.explanation: Hot land creates low pressure, and air flows towards it.

activities.title: Winter Monsoon
activities.prompt: What do winter monsoon winds bring to much of Asia?
options: Mostly dry conditions
Heavy monsoon rain
Strong ocean winds
Very warm air
activities.explanation: In winter, the pressure pattern reverses and dry winds blow from land to ocean.

activities.title: Rain on the Ghats
activities.prompt: When moist ocean winds reach the Western Ghats, where does much more rain fall?
options: On the eastern slopes
On the western slopes
On the northern slopes
In the inland valleys
activities.explanation: The Western Ghats act as a natural barrier, giving their western slopes much more rainfall.

activities.title: Winter Rain
activities.prompt: Some winter monsoon winds collect moisture. Where can they bring rainfall?
options: Eastern and southern India
The western Ghats only
The dry northern interior
Northern inland Asia
activities.explanation: Some winter monsoon winds bring rainfall to parts of eastern and southern India.

activities.title: The Summer Monsoon Process
activities.prompt: Put the summer monsoon process in order.
items: Hot Asian land creates low pressure.
Air flows from high pressure towards low pressure.
Ocean winds carry moisture over warmer land.
activities.explanation: Heating and pressure start the flow that brings moisture and heavy rain.

activities.prompt: A hot summer field lies next to the sea. The sea stays cooler than the field. Monsoon winds blow across the area. What will the wind most likely bring to the field?
options: Dry air blowing from the field out to the sea
Wet air from the sea that brings heavy rain
Still air, because the field and sea are the same heat
Strong wind pushing out, because hot ground pushes air away

why.Dry air blowing from the field out to th: Wrong. This copies the winter pattern, when dry air moves from the land to the sea.
why.Still air, because the field and sea are: Wrong. This thinks land and sea heat the same, but the land heats up faster.
why.Strong wind pushing out, because hot gro: Wrong. This thinks hot ground is high pressure, but hot ground creates low pressure.

activities.explanation: Right. The hot field is low pressure, so moist sea air flows in and brings heavy rain.

activities.prompt: In winter, the land cools faster than the ocean. A farmer checks the wind on a winter morning. What wind direction and weather should the farmer expect?
options: Wind blows from the sea to the land, bringing heavy rain
Wind blows from the land to the sea, bringing heavy rain
Wind blows from the sea to the land, bringing dry weather
Wind blows from the land to the sea, bringing dry weather

why.Wind blows from the sea to the land, bri: Wrong. This keeps the summer wind direction, but in winter the pattern reverses.
why.Wind blows from the land to the sea, bri: Wrong. This thinks winter winds bring heavy rain, but they are mostly dry.
why.Wind blows from the sea to the land, bri: Wrong. This gets the direction backwards, because winter wind blows from the land.

activities.explanation: Right. The land cools faster, so winds blow from the land to the sea and bring dry weather.

activities.prompt: A map shows heavy rain on the western slopes of a mountain range. The eastern slopes are much drier. What best explains this difference?
options: The eastern slopes are closer to the sun than the west
The western slopes are nearer the sea, so they always get more rain
The mountains block moist winds, so the western side gets more rain
The eastern slopes are higher, so the rain falls on the west first

why.The eastern slopes are closer to the sun: Wrong. This thinks distance from the sun decides rain, but the mountains explain the map.
why.The western slopes are nearer the sea, s: Wrong. This thinks being near the sea always brings more rain, but the mountains change where rain falls.
why.The eastern slopes are higher, so the ra: Wrong. This thinks height decides where rain falls, but the mountains block winds on the west side.

activities.explanation: Right. The mountains stop the moist winds on the western side, so it gets more rain.

activities.prompt: Two rooms share an open door. Room X has high pressure air. Room Y has low pressure air. Which way will the air move through the door?
options: From room X to room Y, because air flows from high to low pressure
From room Y to room X, because low pressure air is stronger
Air does not move, because both rooms are full of air
Air moves both ways at the same time through the door

why.From room Y to room X, because low press: Wrong. This reverses the rule and thinks low pressure is the stronger push.
why.Air does not move, because both rooms ar: Wrong. This thinks air stays still when rooms are full of air, but pressure differences still move it.
why.Air moves both ways at the same time thr: Wrong. This thinks both rooms push equally, but one room has higher pressure.

activities.explanation: Right. Room X has higher pressure, so air moves through the door into room Y.

lessons.title: Climate, Our Lives and Disasters

activities.prompt: How does the weather shape our food, water, work, and celebrations?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Weather and Daily Life
activities.body: India has many festivals linked with seasons and farming work. Poor rainfall during the monsoon can harm farming and make people walk for water. It can also make food costlier. Industrial work needs predictable weather and available water. Climate disasters can harm lives, farming, infrastructure and local economies.
keyPoints: Poor monsoon rainfall can harm farming and make people walk for water.
Industrial work needs predictable weather and available water.
Climate disasters can harm lives, agriculture and local economies.
activities.explanation: Weather and water affect farming, work and daily life.

activities.prompt: The monsoon rain did not come well this year. The village well is almost dry. What might happen next?
steps: Poor monsoon rain means the fields get less water, so farming suffers.
Farm workers may move to cities, because there is less farm work in the village.
Poor rain can make food costlier, so families have less money to spend.
People may also walk far for water, so one poor rain harms many lives.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: How Climate Disasters Happen
activities.body: Climate disasters can harm people, agriculture, infrastructure and local economies. A cyclone may form over the sea when intense low pressure attracts moist air. Its cloudless centre is called the eye. Floods cover normally dry land. Landslides are sudden collapses of rock, soil or debris. Forest fires spread rapidly across vegetation.
keyPoints: Disasters harm lives, agriculture, infrastructure and local economies.
Cyclones have a cloudless centre called the eye.
Floods, landslides and forest fires happen in different ways.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect different climate disasters with their effects.

activities.prompt: Which connection is shown by festivals in India?
options: Seasons and farming work
Cities and factories
Monsoons and floods
Fires and cyclones
activities.explanation: Festivals in India are linked with seasons and farming work.

activities.prompt: Poor monsoon rainfall can make people walk long distances for water.
activities.explanation: Poor monsoon rainfall can make people walk long distances for water.

activities.prompt: Industrial activity often depends on ______ weather and available water.
activities.hint: This word means you can depend on it.
activities.explanation: Industrial activity often depends on predictable weather and available water.

pairs: Has a cloudless centre called the eye
Water overflows into normally dry land
Rock, soil or debris suddenly collapses

activities.prompt: Put the steps for a cyclone forming over the sea in order.
items: Intense low pressure forms over the sea
The low pressure attracts moist air
activities.explanation: A cyclone can form when intense low pressure attracts moist air.

activities.prompt: Which set shows the areas harmed by climate disasters?
options: Lives, agriculture, infrastructure, local economies
Lives, agriculture, infrastructure, forests
Lives, factories, infrastructure, local economies
Lives, agriculture, festivals, local economies
activities.explanation: Climate disasters harm lives, agriculture, infrastructure and local economies.

activities.prompt: A village had poor monsoon rain this year. Its fields are very dry now. What is most likely to happen to the farmers?
options: Their crops will grow faster in the dry fields.
Their crops will suffer, so they earn less money.
They will need fewer seeds, so they save money.
The rain will fill the fields with extra water.

why.Their crops will grow faster in the dry: Mistake: thinking less water helps crops grow. Poor rain makes agriculture suffer.
why.They will need fewer seeds, so they save: Mistake: thinking saving seeds saves money. The farmers' crops are still harmed.
why.The rain will fill the fields with extra: Mistake: thinking poor rain adds water. Poor rain means less water arrives.

activities.explanation: Right: poor monsoon rain makes agriculture suffer. Less farming means less money.

activities.prompt: A village sign shows river water on fields. Those fields are usually dry land. What does this sign tell us?
options: The river overflowed onto dry land, so a flood happened.
The land turned into a lake and will stay that way forever.
A cyclone formed over the land and pushed the water up.
The river dried up and the water moved to the fields.

why.The land turned into a lake and will sta: Mistake: thinking flood water always stays forever. The sign shows the water arrived, not that it stays.
why.A cyclone formed over the land and pushe: Mistake: thinking cyclones cause every flood. The sign shows water spread over dry land.
why.The river dried up and the water moved t: Mistake: thinking water moves to fields when a river dries up. The river overflowed; it did not dry.

activities.explanation: Right: a flood is when water overflows onto normally dry land.

activities.prompt: A family lives below a steep hill. After heavy rain, they move to a safer place. Why did they move?
options: The hill was growing taller every year because of trees.
Soil and rock on the hill could suddenly collapse on their home.
They wanted a bigger house with a nicer view.
Heavy rain made the trees on the hill grow very fast.

why.The hill was growing taller every year b: Mistake: thinking hills grow taller. Their danger comes from falling soil, not height.
why.They wanted a bigger house with a nicer: Mistake: thinking people move only for comfort. This family moved to stay safe.
why.Heavy rain made the trees on the hill gr: Mistake: thinking fast-growing trees cause danger. The danger came from soil and rock.

activities.explanation: Right: a landslide is the sudden collapse of rock, soil or debris.

activities.prompt: A factory in a town needs steady weather and water each day. After many dry months, the factory slows its work. Why?
options: Factories do not need water, so dry months do not matter.
Industry depends on steady weather and available water, so work slows.
Factories only make food, so only farms are affected.
Dry months make the factory's machines work faster.

why.Factories do not need water, so dry mont: Mistake: thinking factories never need water. Factories often depend on available water.
why.Factories only make food, so only farms: Mistake: thinking only farms depend on water and weather. Factories depend on them too.
why.Dry months make the factory's machines w: Mistake: thinking dry weather makes machines faster. Factories need steady weather and water.

activities.explanation: Right: industry often depends on predictable weather and available water.

lessons.title: Climate Change

activities.prompt: Why is our planet changing so quickly, and how can we help?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Climate Change
activities.body: Climate change means significant, long-term changes in temperature, rain and weather events. It can work across a whole planet or within one region. Natural processes shaped climate over past millennia. Since the 19th century, human activities have largely driven climate change. The greenhouse effect traps heat. Extra greenhouse gases trap more heat, causing rapid global warming. Mitigation means cutting emissions, planting trees and using renewable energy.
keyPoints: Climate change can affect a planet or a region.
Human activities have largely driven climate change since the 19th century.
The greenhouse effect traps heat and supports life.
Mitigation includes cutting emissions, planting trees and boosting renewable energy.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects climate change, its causes, effects and possible responses.

activities.prompt: One day in summer feels very hot. Is that climate change?
steps: One hot day is weather, because it lasts only a short time.
Climate change means long-term changes in temperature and rain.
Long-term changes take many years to show clearly.
So one hot day alone does not prove climate change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: Which option best means climate change?
options: Short-lived changes in weather
Changes only in one region
Long-term changes in climate
Changes only in temperature
activities.explanation: Climate change means significant, long-term changes in climate.

activities.prompt: Since the 19th century, ______ activities have largely driven climate change.
activities.hint: These activities come from people.
activities.explanation: Human activities have largely driven climate change since the 19th century.

activities.prompt: Which group lists only important causes of climate change?
options: Burning fossil fuels; planting trees; renewable energy
Burning fossil fuels; deforestation; harmful industrial practices
Planting trees; renewable energy; cutting greenhouse gas emissions
Burning fossil fuels; cutting emissions; planting trees
activities.explanation: Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and harmful industrial practices are important causes.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These meanings describe climate change, the greenhouse effect and climate mitigation.

activities.prompt: Put these stages in their correct order.
items: Natural processes drive climate change over past millennia
Human activities drive climate change since the 19th century
activities.explanation: The timeline moves from natural drivers to human-driven rapid warming.

activities.prompt: Which chain best explains rapid global warming?
options: Human activities release gases; extra heat is trapped; global warming follows.
Human activities release gases; extra heat escapes; global warming follows.
Natural processes release gases; extra heat is trapped; global warming follows.
Human activities release gases; extra heat is trapped; global cooling follows.
activities.explanation: Human activities released enormous greenhouse gas amounts. This trapped extra heat and caused rapid global warming.

activities.prompt: Ravi's village has always had rain in July. Now the rain comes in May. Farmers still plant in June, so their crops fail. Why?
options: The farmers were lazy and did not water their crops enough.
Global warming disrupts rain patterns that plants and farmers had adapted to.
Rain in May is always bad for every kind of crop.
Crops need no water in June, so the rain was not needed.

why.The farmers were lazy and did not water: Blames the farmers, but the rain itself changed.
why.Rain in May is always bad for every kind: Thinks rain in one month is bad for all crops, which is not true.
why.Crops need no water in June, so the rain: Thinks crops need no water in June, which misses the change in rain.

activities.explanation: Right: global warming changes the rain times that crops depend on.

activities.prompt: Long ago, the climate changed because of natural processes. Today, the climate is changing again. Why is today's change different?
options: Today's change is faster only because more people now notice the weather.
Nature has stopped causing any change, so humans are the only cause.
Human activities now largely drive change, unlike the natural changes of the past.
Climate has always changed, so today's change is no different at all.

why.Today's change is faster only because mo: Confuses noticing change with causing it. People noticing does not make it faster.
why.Nature has stopped causing any change, s: Overstates: it says nature stopped and humans are the only cause.
why.Climate has always changed, so today's c: Mixes up: a climate changing before does not mean today's change is the same.

activities.explanation: Right: human activities largely drive today's change, unlike natural causes long ago.

activities.prompt: A news report says our town was very hot on one day. A climate study shows temperatures rising over many years. Which evidence best shows climate change?
options: One very hot day, because it was the hottest day this year.
A hot day in the news, because newspapers report only big events.
Temperatures rising over many years, because climate change is long-term.
One cold week, because cold weeks show the Earth is cooling down.

why.One very hot day, because it was the hot: Picks one day, but one day is weather, not long-term climate change.
why.A hot day in the news, because newspaper: Trusts one news story, but a single story cannot show a long-term change.
why.One cold week, because cold weeks show t: Thinks a cold week proves cooling, but one cold week is only weather.

activities.explanation: Right: climate change is long-term, so many years of rising temperatures show it.

activities.prompt: Ananya says trapped heat is always bad for Earth. Her teacher says she is only partly right. Why?
options: Some trapped heat is needed, but extra heat added very fast harms.
Trapped heat is always bad for every living thing on Earth.
Heat never gets trapped, so her idea has no real meaning at all.
Trapped heat only matters during the cold winter months, not summer.

why.Trapped heat is always bad for every liv: Thinks all trapped heat is bad, forgetting Earth needs some warmth to support life.
why.Heat never gets trapped, so her idea has: Thinks heat is never trapped, which goes against how the natural greenhouse effect works.
why.Trapped heat only matters during the col: Thinks heat matters only in winter, which misses how trapped heat works.

activities.explanation: Right: some trapped heat warms Earth for life, but sudden extra heat causes rapid warming.

activities.context: In a village in India, farmers wait for the monsoon before they sow seeds. This year the rain arrived later than usual, and a farmer worried that his crop would suffer. The village elders said the weather changes from hour to hour, so one unusual day is not a pattern. The region's climate, the long-term pattern of its weather, still follows the same yearly rhythm. Soon afterwards, a festival linked with the season was celebrated as usual.
activities.prompt: The monsoon rain was late this year. Which statement best explains what the farmer should understand?
options: Late rain shows the region's climate has permanently shifted, so the village should expect this every year.
One late season is a short-term weather change, while climate describes a region's weather over many years.
The Earth has moved closer to the Sun, so the monsoon will always arrive later from now on.
The farmer should check the rain only once a year, since weather matters only during festivals.

why.Late rain shows the region's climate has: Wrong: this confuses one season's rain with climate. Recent climate changes come from human actions, not one late monsoon.
why.The Earth has moved closer to the Sun, s: Wrong: seasons come from the Earth revolving around the Sun, and one late monsoon does not change that.
why.The farmer should check the rain only on: Wrong: weather changes from hour to hour and matters for farming, not only for festivals.

activities.explanation: Correct: weather can change quickly, while climate is the long-term pattern of a region's weather.

activities.context: In a village in India, farmers wait for the monsoon before they sow seeds. This year the rain arrived later than usual, and a farmer worried that his crop would suffer. The village elders said the weather changes from hour to hour, so one unusual day is not a pattern. The region's climate, the long-term pattern of its weather, still follows the same yearly rhythm. Soon afterwards, a festival linked with the season was celebrated as usual.
activities.prompt: Why was the festival still celebrated as usual even though the rain was late?
options: The festival was moved to the day the rain started, so the farmers could join in.
The Earth stopped revolving around the Sun during the late rain, so the season paused.
The festival is tied to a season that recurs annually, so its timing rests on the season rather than one rain.
The late rain was counted as the start of a new season, so the festival came early.

why.The festival was moved to the day the ra: Wrong: festivals are linked with seasons, not with the first day of rain.
why.The Earth stopped revolving around the S: Wrong: the Earth keeps revolving around the Sun, and that movement is what causes seasons.
why.The late rain was counted as the start o: Wrong: one late rain does not start a new season; seasons follow their cycle.

activities.explanation: Correct: the season returns each year, so the festival linked to it stays on schedule.

activities.prompt: How does the seasonal cycle affect the life of plants and animals and the festivals of the six ṛitus?
activities.answer: Seasons occur because the Earth revolves around the Sun, and they return in a cycle. Plant and animal life follows this rhythm, so living things change with each season. Many parts of India divide the year into six ṛitus, and festivals are linked with them.
points: Seasons occur because the Earth revolves around the Sun
Seasons return in a cycle
Plant and animal life follows the seasonal rhythm
Many parts of India have six ṛitus, linked with rituals and festivals
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a tropical climate and a subtropical climate?
activities.answer: Both names relate to the tropics, two special parallels of latitude. A tropical climate has distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds, as in eastern India and the southern peninsula. A subtropical climate, like the northern plains, has very hot summers and cold winters.
points: Both terms relate to the tropics, which are two parallels of latitude
Tropical climate has distinct wet and dry periods controlled by monsoon winds
Subtropical climate has very hot summers and cold winters
Examples: eastern India and southern peninsula (tropical) vs northern plains (subtropical)
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family moved from a coastal town to a village far inland. In the village, summer afternoons feel much hotter, and winter nights feel much colder than they did by the sea. Their cousin lives on a mountain slope, where the air feels thin and chilly even at noon. He says he needs a jacket there, although the sky is clear and the sun is out.
activities.prompt: If the family moved back to the coastal town, what would most likely happen to the difference between summer and winter temperatures?
options: Summers would become cooler, because the coast lies at a higher altitude than the village.
Winters would become much colder, because coastal air is thinner and lighter than inland air.
Seasonal temperature differences would shrink, since the sea keeps temperatures more moderate.
Seasonal temperature differences would grow, since the family would be farther from sea moisture.

why.Summers would become cooler, because the: Wrong: the case never says the coast is higher than the village.
why.Winters would become much colder, becaus: Wrong: thin, light air comes with height, not with living near the coast.
why.Seasonal temperature differences would g: Wrong: moving to the coast brings the family closer to the sea, not farther from it.

activities.explanation: Right: temperatures become less extreme near the coast than far inland.

activities.context: A family moved from a coastal town to a village far inland. In the village, summer afternoons feel much hotter, and winter nights feel much colder than they did by the sea. Their cousin lives on a mountain slope, where the air feels thin and chilly even at noon. He says he needs a jacket there, although the sky is clear and the sun is out.
activities.prompt: The family plans to visit the cousin's slope in winter. What should they pack, and why?
options: Pack only sunscreen and sandals, because strong sun keeps high places warm all day.
Pack warm layers, because the slope is high and cold increases with height.
Pack heavy rain gear only, because mountain air always brings rain from the sea.
Pack the same clothes as at the coast, because the slope shares coastal temperatures.

why.Pack only sunscreen and sandals, because: Wrong: strong sun does not keep a high place warm; the slope is cold.
why.Pack heavy rain gear only, because mount: Wrong: rain depends on sea winds, and the case does not say the slope gets them.
why.Pack the same clothes as at the coast, b: Wrong: the slope does not share coastal temperatures, since temperatures are more extreme inland.

activities.explanation: Right: higher ground is colder, so warm clothes are needed.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Western Ghats give their western slopes much more rainfall.
activities.answer: Ocean winds carry moisture from the sea. The Western Ghats act as a natural barrier, so the moisture-carrying winds are held back on the western side. This moisture condenses over the land and falls as heavy rain, so the western slopes get much more rainfall than the rest of the area.
points: Ocean winds carry moisture from the sea
The Western Ghats act as a natural barrier
The barrier holds back the moisture-carrying winds on the western side
The moisture condenses and falls as heavy rain on the western slopes
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a cyclone and a flood?
activities.answer: A cyclone forms when intense low pressure over the sea attracts moist air. A flood occurs when water overflows into normally dry land. So a cyclone is a storm that forms over the sea, while a flood is water spreading over land that is usually dry.
points: A cyclone forms over the sea from intense low pressure and moist air
A flood is water overflowing onto normally dry land
A cyclone is a storm system, while a flood is an overflow of water
Clear contrast of origin: a storm over the sea versus water spreading over land
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the warming seen today is different from the climate change that happened during past millennia.
activities.answer: Natural processes drove climate change during past millennia, and carbon was released gradually. Since the 19th century, human activities have released enormous amounts of greenhouse gases in only a few centuries. This sudden increase traps extra heat, so global warming happens rapidly today.
points: Past climate change was driven by natural processes
Carbon and gases were released gradually in the natural carbon cycle
Human activities since the 19th century released huge amounts of greenhouse gases quickly
This sudden increase traps extra heat, causing rapid global warming
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Which statement about weather and climate is correct?
options: Climate is the short-term weather at one hour.
Climate is the long-term weather pattern of a region.
Weather is the long-term pattern of a region's climate.
Weather is a region's yearly pattern of rainfall.
activities.explanation: Weather changes hourly. Climate shows a region's long-term weather pattern.

activities.prompt: What causes seasons to occur each year?
options: Earth stays still beside the Sun
The Sun circles Earth slowly
Earth revolves around the Sun
Earth moves farther from the Sun
activities.explanation: Earth revolves around the Sun, so seasons occur. Each season lasts a few months and returns yearly.

activities.prompt: Match each climate clue to the place it describes.
pairs: Extremely hot days and cool nights
Very hot summers and cold winters
activities.explanation: These places have different temperature, rainfall and moisture patterns.

activities.prompt: The Western Ghats act as a natural barrier. Where do they give much more rainfall?
options: On their western slopes
On their eastern slopes
On both slopes equally
Away from their slopes
activities.explanation: The Western Ghats act as a barrier. Their western slopes receive much more rainfall.

activities.prompt: As altitude increases, temperature ______.
activities.hint: It gets lower as you climb higher.
activities.explanation: Temperature decreases as altitude increases. Higher places are cooler than lower places.

activities.prompt: Put the summer monsoon process in order.
activities.explanation: Hot land creates low pressure. Moist ocean winds then bring heavy monsoon rain.

activities.prompt: The cloudless centre of a cyclone is called its eye.
activities.explanation: Yes. A cyclone can form when intense low pressure attracts moist air. Its centre is called the eye.

activities.prompt: A landslide is a burst of uncontrolled fire across vegetation.
activities.explanation: A landslide is the sudden collapse of rock, soil or debris. Forest fires are uncontrolled fires across vegetation.

activities.prompt: Match each action or process with its correct meaning.
pairs: A major driver of climate change
An important cause of climate change
activities.explanation: Human actions drive recent climate change. Planting trees and renewable energy can help reduce it.

activities.prompt: Put the effects of extra greenhouse gases in order.
items: Adapted plants, animals and societies face disruption
activities.explanation: Extra trapped heat causes global warming. This disrupts climate patterns.
